newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Port problems compound Argentine maize blues.
newsitem.headline: Port problems compound Argentine maize blues.

text.p: Big delays in a major southern Argentine grain port are heaping further problems on the shoulders of Argentina's maize exporters, who are already carrying the burden of high prices relative to U.S. grain.

The port of Necochea in southern Buenos Aires province will probably be closed until Saturday or Sunday due to a heavy swell, compounding delays caused by a build up of silt in the main access channel. Nine ships are stuck in port and 20 are waiting to enter, port authorities said Friday.
"There's a queue of ships which stretches as far as Ecuador," said one disgruntled trader in Buenos Aires.

He explained that Argentine maize, offered at about $107 FOB for July or July/August shipping, was already about five dollars more expensive than the U.S. product, and Necochea's woes were scaring off the few otherwise willing buyers.
"There's no one enquiring about maize. We had a call from Malaysia, but they did not like the price," he said.

"Part of the problem is the impossibility of completing the ships in Necochea," he added, "It's only going to be worth anyone's while to buy in ships of 50,000-60,000 tonnes, and they can't get in through the access channel."
He said that most of Argentina's remaining available maize was in the area of Necochea.
"If you sell to an export destination today, their ships are going to have to wait 20 days in Necochea with the backlog. And that's effectively going to add $5 a tonne," he said.

But traders agreed that the main problem for selling Argentine maize is that farmers are not prepared to drop their prices on the cash market enough to compete with U.S. corn exporters, who are rich in grain and in an aggressive mood.
"This comes after we started the season selling maize extremely quickly. We sold to a pile of destinations we hadn't touched the season before," an another trader said, "like Indonesia and Malaysia."

Traders said they thought Argentina had sold about 7.0-7.5 million tonnes of 1996/97 maize to export buyers, with about 6.8 million tonnes already shipped. The biggest buyer has been South Korea, taking about 2.0 million tonnes.

This would leave 2.5-3.0 million tonnes still to move on export markets. While this looks difficult at today's prices, traders felt that most farmers did not have the financial capacity to store their grain for long and would eventually be forced to drop their prices.
But at the moment the list of possible buyers is short, starting with Iran.

"There's Iran, which doesn't buy American. Maybe Cuba, or Peru or Chile," a trader said. He added Iran had taken about 800,000 tonnes of Argentine maize so far and would probably try and get by without any more until its own new crop.
The problems at Necochea are also hitting late season wheat sales to Brazil.
"The only port where there is bread wheat to sell is Necochea, and the Brazilians don't want to wait 10 days," a trader said.
Traders said that export wheat sales so far totaled over eight million tonnes, leaving a bit less than two million tonnes still to move.

The Necochea port's general manager Jose Maria Saravia told Reuters that it was on the verge of clinching an Inter-American Development Bank loan to fund a $38 million plan to improve channel access and cut the number of days lost a year. Dredge work to clear the channel will start when the port reopens.
The port, which moved 3.2 million tonnes of grains in the first six months of the year, is usually closed about 15 percent of the year.
((--Buenos Aires Newsroom +541 318-0655))
